lessons.title: Your place in the small stock abattoir
lessons.html:
Working as a team

On a sheep and goat line, many people work on each carcass: the lairage hand, the stunner, the sticker, the leggers and skinners, the eviscerator, the trimmer, the weigher and the chiller team. Each person's work affects the next person. A careless skinner who leaves wool on the meat makes extra work for the trimmer, and may cost the farmer money.

What makes a good team member

  • Be on time and ready to start when the first animal comes through.
  • Do your share of the work, at the right standard.
  • Help others when they fall behind, if you are trained for their task.
  • Respect everyone: no swearing, fighting, bullying or harassment. Treat people of all languages, cultures and genders with respect.
  • Be honest: report mistakes, injuries and damage. Never take meat, offal, skins or tools without permission.

Rights and responsibilities

You have the right to fair treatment, a payslip, leave and a safe workplace. You also have responsibilities: to follow the company rules, to work safely and to look after the safety of others. The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires workers to follow safety rules and report unsafe conditions.

If you have a problem, speak to your supervisor first. If it is not solved, use your company's grievance procedure. Know who your shop steward or worker representative is, if there is one.

lessons.title: Communication, numbers and records on the line
lessons.html:
Communicating in a noisy place

  • Face the person and speak clearly.
  • Keep messages short.
  • Repeat important instructions back to check you understood.
  • Use the hand signals your plant uses, for example for stopping the line.
  • Shout a clear warning if someone is in danger.

Using numbers at work

  • Counting animals at receiving and in the lairage.
  • Carcass numbers: matching heads, organs and carcasses.
  • Mass: lamb carcasses are weighed in kilograms (kg).
  • Time: shift times, break times, overtime.
  • Money: checking your payslip in rand.

Example: A farmer brings 120 lambs. 115 are slaughtered on Monday and the rest on Tuesday. How many on Tuesday? 120 minus 115 equals 5.

Example: 4 lamb carcasses weigh 18 kg, 20 kg, 19 kg and 21 kg. Total: 78 kg.

Records

You may fill in receiving sheets, lairage counts, cleaning checklists or temperature logs.

  1. Use a pen and write clearly.
  2. Write the date and time.
  3. Record what really happened, after the task is done.
  4. Sign your name.

A false record can lead to unsafe meat or unfair payment to a farmer. It is a serious offence.

lessons.title: Looking after yourself and growing
lessons.html:
Your health

Slaughtering sheep and goats is hard, physical work with knives, wet floors and cold rooms.

  • Eat well and drink water during breaks.
  • Get enough sleep. Tired people make mistakes and cut themselves.
  • Never come to work under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
  • Report illness, such as diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or skin sores, before your shift.
  • Report pain in your hands, wrists, shoulders or back early.
  • Some animal diseases can spread to people. Wash your hands well and cover cuts.

If you are stressed or have personal problems, ask whether your company has an employee wellness programme, or speak to a clinic, a social worker or someone you trust.

Managing money

  • Make a monthly budget: income first, then the things you must pay, such as food, rent, transport and school fees.
  • Save a little every month, even R50.
  • Be careful of loan sharks and high-interest loans. Read contracts before signing.

Growing your career

A small stock slaughterer can learn every station: lairage, stunning, legging, skinning, evisceration, offal, trimming and chilling. Later you can become a team leader, supervisor, classifier, or study further, for example in meat examination.

  • Do your job well and be reliable.
  • Ask to learn new stations.
  • Finish your training and keep your certificates safe.
  • Set a clear goal and a date to reach it.

Key points

  • Every worker on the line affects the next; do your share well.
  • Be on time, honest and respectful.
  • Repeat important instructions back to check you understood.
  • Fill in records truthfully after the task is done.
  • Report illness before work and never work under the influence.
  • Budget your pay and set goals to grow your career.
